Sup
SUP
verb
From the Old English sūpan, “to sip, to swallow,” reinforced by the Old French souper; hence to take the evening meal, to eat supper — the settled, unhurried table at the end of the day’s work.

Biblical Definition

To sup is to take supper — not a snatched bite but the evening meal, the long table when the work is done, the meal of intimacy and rest. The word keeps its household plainness: the master says to the servant come in from the field, “Make ready wherewith I may sup, and gird thyself, and serve me” (Luk 17:8), and our Lord uses it to teach that the servant claims no thanks for doing what was commanded. It marks the holiest table in Scripture’s history: “After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood” (1Co 11:25). The cup came after supper — the paschal meal finished, the old covenant fulfilled at its own table, and a new testament in His blood set in its place. From that night the church has supped at the Lord’s table, where Christ is truly present to faith and feeds His people, though the bread be bread still. Then the word rises to the promise: “Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me” (Rev 3:20). To a lukewarm church that had shut her Lord outside, Christ offers not a rebuke only but a supper. And the whole of it runs toward one board at the end of history: “Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Rev 19:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

To take the evening meal; to eat supper; the settled table of rest and fellowship at day’s end.

expand to see more

SUP, to take supper; to eat the evening repast.

From the Saxon sūpan, “to sip, to swallow,” and Old French souper.

It denotes the settled meal at the end of labour, not a hasty bite.

Christ took the cup when He had supped, instituting the new testament (1Co 11:25).

He offers to come in and sup with him that opens the door (Rev 3:20).

Key Scripture

Luk 17:8 — "And will not rather say unto him, Make ready wherewith I may sup, and gird thyself, and serve me, till I have eaten and drunken; and afterward thou shalt eat and drink?"

1Co 11:25 — "After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me."

Rev 3:20 — "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me."

Rev 19:9 — "And he saith unto me, Write, Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb. And he saith unto me, These are the true sayings of God."

Modern Corruption

A live corruption of one verse: Rev 3:20 is a summons to a lukewarm church, not a sentimental proof-text for the sinner’s decision to let Christ in.

expand to see more

No verse with this word has been wrenched further from its place than Revelation 3:20. It is preached as though Christ stood powerless outside the unbeliever’s heart, waiting on a decision He cannot make and hoping for a latch He cannot lift — the whole of salvation hanging on the creature’s turn of the handle. But read the address: this letter is written to the church at Laodicea, lukewarm, rich and increased with goods, that had put her own Lord out of doors. The knocking is Christ recalling a backslidden congregation to His table, not a Saviour begging admission to a heart He is unable to enter. Scripture nowhere leaves the door in the sinner’s hand: the LORD opened Lydia’s heart, that she attended unto the things spoken of Paul, and the same effectual grace opens every door that opens at all.

Restore the verse and it grows greater, not smaller. The Christ who knocks is the sovereign Lord who counsels Laodicea to buy of Him gold tried in the fire and white raiment; He rebukes and chastens whom He loves; and the door that opens, opens because He gave the hearing ear to the voice outside it. Then the promise is not a bargain but a banquet: I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me — the long evening table, the meal of rest and intimacy with the risen Christ, pledged now at the Lord’s Supper and consummated at the marriage supper of the Lamb. He does not knock to be let in on our terms; He knocks because He has determined to sup.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to take the evening meal, the settled table of rest and fellowship.

Sup — Old English sūpan, “to sip, to swallow.”

Reinforced by Old French souper, “to take the evening meal.”

It denotes the unhurried table when the day’s labour is done.

The cup of the new testament was taken when He had supped (1Co 11:25).

Christ promises to come in and sup with him that opens (Rev 3:20).

Usage

"He took the cup when He had supped: the paschal table finished, the new testament begun."

"Rev 3:20 knocks at a lukewarm church’s door, not at a heart that can open itself."

"Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb."
